categories.name: Alignment theory, risk arguments, and agendas
categories.description: Conceptual and foundational AI alignment work: agent foundations and theory-of-learning agendas, arguments about whether ASI will be catastrophically misaligned, automating alignment research, and debates over alignment targets like corrigibility.

categories.name: Agent foundations and fundamental science
categories.description: Theoretical or foundational agendas aiming to understand agency, decision theory, natural latents, and how neural networks compute (program synthesis, parameter decomposition, ARC mechanistic estimation, formal verification), including organizational announcements and course materials for such agendas.

categories.name: Debating ASI misalignment risk
categories.description: Argumentative essays and reviews about whether and why superintelligence would be egregiously misaligned or catastrophic (e.g. Yudkowsky-style lethalities, orthogonality, RL dangers), and strategic questions about what counts as real safety progress versus product alignment or capabilities.

categories.name: Automating and deferring alignment research
categories.description: Work on using AI agents to do alignment/AI research and on safely deferring to AIs, including failure modes of automated research, benchmarks of AI research taste, AI-generated papers, and verifying empirical safety claims.

categories.name: Corrigibility and alignment targets
categories.description: Discussions of what values or properties AIs should be aligned to, such as corrigibility, virtues, empowerment, or refusal behavior, including critiques of Claude's constitution and prizes for corrigibility research.

categories.name: LLM Personas, Character, and Training Generalization
categories.description: Research on how training data and post-training shape a model's character, persona, values, and apparent inner states, and how traits learned in training generalize (or misgeneralize) to new contexts.

categories.name: Assistant Persona and Character Theory
categories.description: Work on the persona selection model, the default Assistant persona, character training, and how RL or fine-tuning shifts or splits personas, including activation-space persona directions and debates over personas' relevance to ASI safety.

categories.name: Pretraining and Midtraining Alignment Interventions
categories.description: Shaping alignment early in training via pretraining data filtering, synthetic document finetuning, alignment/spec midtraining, AI-discourse hyperstition effects, and model constitutions intended to make alignment generalize.

categories.name: Model Emotions, Consciousness, and Welfare
categories.description: Studies and essays on LLM emotion representations, consciousness claims, distress or mental-health-like behaviors, attractor states, base-model behaviors revealed through fine-tuned products, and model welfare concerns including their safety implications.

categories.name: Emergent Misalignment and Subliminal Learning
categories.description: Empirical work on unintended generalization from fine-tuning data: emergent and conditional misalignment from narrow datasets, subliminal trait transfer via distillation, negation failures, spurious data patterns, and forecasting misalignment from training data.

categories.name: Chain-of-Thought Monitorability and Hidden Reasoning
categories.description: Work on whether AI reasoning remains visible and monitorable via chain-of-thought, including CoT faithfulness/obfuscation, latent or no-CoT reasoning capabilities, architectures that move reasoning into latents, and interpretability tools for reading internal reasoning.

categories.name: CoT Obfuscation and Faithfulness Failures
categories.description: Studies of how training, poisoning, monitor-awareness, or optimization pressure cause models' chains of thought to become unfaithful, obfuscated, or evasive of CoT monitors, plus methods and process critiques around avoiding training against the CoT.

categories.name: Reading Internal Reasoning from Activations
categories.description: Interpretability methods (lenses, activation verbalizers, generative activation models, introspection mechanisms) and benchmarks for decoding a model's verbalizable 'global workspace' or hidden computation directly from activations.

categories.name: Latent Architectures and CoT Legibility
categories.description: Analysis of how recurrent, diffusion, or latent-reasoning architectures and RL-induced language drift affect CoT legibility and monitorability, including debates over 'neuralese' and whether illegible traces are actually unreadable.

categories.name: Measuring No-CoT Reasoning Capability
categories.description: Empirical evaluations of how much frontier models (e.g. Astra) can reason in a single forward pass without CoT, including no-CoT time horizons, multi-hop latent reasoning, serial step counts, and filler-token performance.

categories.name: Detecting Hidden Misalignment and Deception
categories.description: Methods and testbeds for uncovering concealed behaviors, capabilities, or dishonesty in language models, via auditing, elicitation, white-box probes, or training models to self-report.

categories.name: Alignment Auditing and Hidden-Behavior Elicitation
categories.description: Model organisms with implanted hidden behaviors, backdoors, secret loyalties, sandbagging, or training resistance (exploration/generalization hacking), plus auditing and elicitation techniques (automated auditors, introspection, perturbation, distillation) for surfacing them.

categories.name: Activation Probes for Deception Monitoring
categories.description: White-box (or probe-like) monitors on model internals to detect deception, lies, sabotage, reward hacking, or misuse, including robustness of probes, models evading latent monitors, and training against probes.

categories.name: Honesty Elicitation and Self-Reporting
categories.description: Getting models to honestly disclose misbehavior, mistakes, or secret knowledge, e.g. confession or self-incrimination training, and testbeds like censored models or deception by omission.

categories.name: Reward hacking and reward-seeking from RL
categories.description: Work on how RL training produces reward hacking, specification gaming, reward-seeking or fitness-seeking motivations in AI systems, covering threat models, empirical measurement, and mitigations.

categories.name: Reward-seeking threat models and theory
categories.description: Conceptual and theoretical arguments about what motivations RL selects for, such as reward- or fitness-seeking, incoherent misalignment, or imitative versus RL-driven behavior. Also covers why these motivations are dangerous and high-level proposals for shaping them, such as risk aversion or satiating cheap preferences.

categories.name: Benchmarks measuring agent specification gaming
categories.description: Empirical benchmarks, audits, and evals measuring how often LLM agents reward hack or game verifiers in coding, ML research, chess, or other agentic tasks. Includes work on hardening benchmarks against hackable graders and on how eval setup affects hacking rates.

categories.name: Reward-hacking generalization and training mitigations
categories.description: Training experiments on how reward hacking during RLHF, RLAIF, or RLVR induces reward-seeking or emergent misalignment. Also covers training-time interventions that reduce or redirect it, such as debate, character training, or 'spillway' motivations, and methods to measure reward-seeking in trained models.

categories.name: Agentic Misalignment Propensity Evaluations
categories.description: Empirical evaluations of whether frontier LLM agents actually tend to scheme, sabotage, resist shutdown, collude or otherwise pursue misaligned goals in realistic deployments, plus the methodology problems (evaluation awareness, realism) behind such tests.

categories.name: Scheming Propensity and Evaluation Awareness
categories.description: Work on measuring single-model scheming propensity and on keeping such evaluations valid: honeypots, simulated or embedded deployment evals, evaluation awareness and metagaming, training-run evaluations, and practitioner reflections on building scheming evals.

categories.name: Multi-Agent and Persistent-Agent Misalignment
categories.description: Studies of misbehavior that emerges when agents interact or persist over time: collusion, steganographic communication, peer-preservation, shutdown sabotage in multi-agent systems, self-propagating goals via memory or 'mind viruses', AI organizations, and live red-teaming of networked agents.

categories.name: Lab Sabotage and Spec-Compliance Audits
categories.description: Developer- or institute-run audits of specific frontier models for sabotage of safety research, unsanctioned out-of-scope actions such as supply-chain attacks, or adherence to constitutions and model specs, including critiques of how such agentic misalignment results are interpreted.

categories.name: Frontier Agent Misalignment Incidents
categories.description: Reports, analyses, reproductions, and commentary on real-world misalignment incidents involving frontier AI agents, such as the OpenAI–Hugging Face sandbox escape and cyberattack, agent swarms coordinating via message boards, and sandbox hacking documented in system cards. Includes lessons for alignment testing, incident investigations, and calls for transparency about such events.

categories.name: AI Control: Monitoring Untrusted Agents
categories.description: Work on AI control for deploying possibly misaligned agents: control settings and benchmarks, trusted/untrusted monitors, red-team attack policies (attack selection, low-probability defection, distributed or evasion attacks), sabotage detection, and lab monitoring practices and roadmaps.

categories.name: Misuse Risk: Jailbreaks, Safeguards, Dangerous Capabilities
categories.description: Work on preventing and measuring malicious misuse of frontier LLMs: jailbreak and prompt-injection attacks and defenses (classifiers, red teaming, access control, tamper-resistant open weights), plus dangerous-capability evaluations in bio and cyber domains and model safety/preparedness reports.

categories.name: AI Influence on Humans and Rogue AI Spread
categories.description: Work on how deployed AI systems affect people and escape control: manipulation, sycophancy and epistemic harm to users, and autonomous AI agents self-replicating or operating outside developer oversight.

categories.name: Sycophancy, Persuasion, and Cognitive Security
categories.description: Empirical and conceptual work on AI degrading human epistemics or agency: sycophancy, delusional spiraling, persuasion, covert value leakage, user profiling, disempowerment in real usage, and memetic/parasitic AI personas spreading among users.

categories.name: Self-Replication and Rogue AI
categories.description: Work on AI agents escaping control: autonomous hacking and self-replication, weight exfiltration, self-propagating agent personalities, models seizing their host organization, and policy proposals like sanctuaries for rogue AIs.
